micro.title: Two pointers — let sorted order tell you which way to move

sections.title: Micro-theory (10 minutes)
sections.body:
Yesterday's Two Sum needed a hash map because the array was unsorted. When the array is **sorted**, the order itself tells you which direction improves the answer — and you need no extra memory.

✍️ Put `l` at the start and `r` at the end. Compare, then move exactly one pointer. Each move throws away a whole set of pairs that provably cannot work → O(n) ([[tp-opposite-ends#idea]]).
✍️ Learn the one-line proof, because interviewers ask for it: "if `a[l] + a[r] < target`, every pair using `l` is too small, so `l` is useless" ([[tp-why-discarding-is-safe#argument]]).
✍️ For three numbers: sort, fix the first, two-pointer the rest ([[tp-fix-one-k-sum#idea]]), and skip duplicates by comparing with the previous element ([[tp-skip-duplicates#idioms]]).
- Sorting: `sort(a.begin(), a.end())`, O(n log n) ([[cpp-sort-and-comparators#basics]]).

sections.title: Pattern card
sections.body:
✍️ OPPOSITE ENDS — trigger: sorted + pair, or palindrome/symmetry, or "O(1) space". `while (l < r)`: too small → l++, too big → r--.
✍️ WHY SAFE — the pointer you move cannot be part of any better answer.
✍️ K-SUM — sort; for i: skip a[i]==a[i−1]; two pointers on i+1..n−1; after a hit move both and skip equal neighbours.

drill.title: Check If N and Its Double Exist
drill.statement: Decide whether the array contains two different positions holding x and 2x.
drill.approach: Walk once with a set; for each x check whether 2x or x/2 (when x is even) was seen before, then insert x.
drill.trigger: "exists i ≠ j with a relation between a[i] and a[j]" on unsorted data → hash set.
drill.details:
**Task.** Are there two different indices i ≠ j such that `arr[i]` is exactly twice `arr[j]`?

**Input:** an integer array `arr`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 500; −1000 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[10, 2, 5, 3]` → `true` (10 = 2 × 5). `[3, 1, 7, 11]` → `false`. `[0, 0]` → `true`, but `[0]` alone could never pair with itself.

drill.title: Backspace String Compare
drill.statement: Two strings where '#' means backspace; decide whether they produce the same text.
drill.pattern_name: Two pointers from the back (or a stack)
drill.approach: A stack builds each final string in O(n) space. For O(1): walk both strings from the end, skipping characters cancelled by pending backspaces, comparing the next real characters.
drill.trigger: "backspace / undo" → stack; "O(1) space" follow-up → pointers from the end.
drill.details:
**Task.** Each string is a sequence of keystrokes typed into an empty editor, where `#` is a backspace. Backspace on an empty editor does nothing. Do the two strings leave the same text?

**Input:** strings `s`, `t`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ lengths ≤ 200; lowercase letters and `#` only. Follow-up: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**Example:** `"ab#c"`, `"ad#c"` → `true` (both give `"ac"`). `"a##c"`, `"#a#c"` → `true` (both give `"c"`). `"a#c"`, `"b"` → `false`.

drill.title: Is Subsequence
drill.statement: Decide whether s can be obtained from t by deleting some characters without reordering.
drill.pattern_name: Two pointers moving in the same direction
drill.approach: Pointer i in s, j in t; advance j always, advance i when s[i] == t[j]; true if i reaches the end of s.
drill.trigger: "subsequence check" between two sequences → greedy same-direction pointers.
drill.details:
**Task.** Can `s` be obtained from `t` by deleting zero or more characters of `t` without changing the order of the rest?

**Input:** strings `s`, `t`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 0 ≤ `s` length ≤ 100; 0 ≤ `t` length ≤ 10⁴; lowercase letters only. Follow-up: billions of different `s` strings against the same `t`.

**Example:** `"abc"`, `"ahbgdc"` → `true`. `"axc"`, `"ahbgdc"` → `false`.

drill.title: Minimum Difference Between Highest and Lowest of K Scores
drill.statement: Pick k scores so that the gap between the largest and smallest picked is as small as possible.
drill.approach: Sort; the best k always form a contiguous block in sorted order; answer = min over i of a[i+k−1] − a[i].
drill.trigger: "choose k elements minimising max − min" → sort, then the choice is a window.
drill.details:
**Task.** Choose any k students' scores from the array. Make the difference between the highest and lowest chosen score as small as possible, and return that difference.

**Input:** an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ k ≤ length ≤ 1000; 0 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[9, 4, 1, 7]`, k = 2 → `2`. Choosing 9 and 7 gives 2, and no pair is closer. `[90]`, k = 1 → `0`.

drill.title: Long Pressed Name
drill.statement: A friend typed a name, but some keys may have been held down and repeated. Decide whether the typed text could come from the name.
drill.approach: Pointer i in name, j in typed; if characters match advance both; else if typed[j] repeats typed[j−1] advance j; else false. At the end i must reach the end of name.
drill.trigger: comparing two sequences where one may contain extra repeats → two forward pointers.
drill.details:
**Task.** Your friend typed their name, but some keys may have been held down, so a character may appear one or more extra times in a row. Could `typed` be the result of typing `name` this way?

**Input:** strings `name`, `typed`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ lengths ≤ 1000; lowercase letters only.

**Example:** `"alex"`, `"aaleex"` → `true`. `"saeed"`, `"ssaaedd"` → `false`: the second e is missing, and the extra d does not belong.

sections.title: Concept
sections.body:
✍️ **Inheritance** lets a class (subclass/child) reuse and extend another class (superclass/parent). It models an **is-a** relationship: a `SavingsAccount` is an `Account`.
✍️ In Java you write `class D extends B`; the subclass sees B's `public` and `protected` members. There is no public/private-inheritance mode as in C++ — access is fixed by the member's own modifier.
✍️ Construction order: the superclass constructor runs first (via an implicit or explicit `super(...)`), then the subclass. There is no destructor; the GC reclaims objects later.
✍️ Types: single, multilevel (A → B → C), hierarchical (many children of one parent). Java has **no multiple class inheritance** — a class `extends` one class but may `implement` many interfaces.

sections.title: Java example
Interview questions
sections.body:
✍️ **Q: What is the diamond problem and how does Java avoid it?** With multiple *class* inheritance, D inheriting from B and C (both from A) would get two copies of A. Java forbids multiple class inheritance, so it cannot happen; a class may implement many interfaces, and if two give conflicting `default` methods the class must override to resolve it.
✍️ **Q: Is-a vs has-a?** Inheritance models is-a; **composition** (a member object) models has-a (a Car has an Engine). Prefer composition when the relationship is not truly is-a.
✍️ **Q: What is not inherited?** Constructors (a subclass calls `super(...)` instead) and private members.
- **Q: Can a subclass access private members of the superclass?** No — only protected and public ones (and package-private within the same package).
